title: Tetra-CORE-der
text:
(and apparently ripe for alliteration!)
Mineral maps are the perfect product for a geologist. They break the core into domains and show, at a glance, the picture of the rock we only build in our heads after years of training. They are immediately interpretable, and they look confident.
They look just as confident when they’re wrong.
If you have heard of hyperspectral data, at a surface level, then a mineral map is what you think of.
There is a wide variety of methods to produce mineral maps, all of them extremely effective under certain conditions, many involving advanced ML techniques, and many are proprietary.
CoreSpecViewer exposes a small subset of Mineral Mapping tools; Pearson correlation, Spectral Angle Mapping and Modified Spectral Angle Mapping (which is functionally Pearson). Pearson correlation measures whether two spectra rise and fall together, ignoring their overall brightness. SAM treats each spectrum as a vector and measures the angle between them. Both reduce the comparison to a single number over the whole wavelength range.
I am only going to talk about one method here; Pearson correlation. I expose a simple winner-takes-all implementation of this method in CoreSpecViewer and the criticisms that I level at this method also applies to the SAM method in CoreSpecViewer, but do not necessarily apply to all mineral maps that you may have access to.






NoteThe example boxes




Box 1: well 13-18-088-11W5, 1590.80–1593.60 m, scanned 2022-02-11.
Box 2: drillhole DH-64-03, Carrowreagh, 0.00–1.00 m, scanned 2026-08-31.

Data sources and licences are listed in the Data section.











Direct mineral mapping against full library


This is the mineral map I produced in my hyperspectral made easy note. The mineral map was produced by Pearson correlation of every pixel in the image against every exemplar in the library. The CoreSpecViewer Pearson winner-takes-all pipeline is multi-step;

take a specified collection from the library,

resample the library spectra to the data wavelength grid, 1
remove the continuum of the library spectra using the same method as for the data,
for each pixel, calculate the correlation coefficient of the continuum removed spectra against each library exemplar, and assign that pixel the value of the exemplar with the highest coefficient,

assign every pixel with a coefficient below a threshold (0.7 by default) a no-result value.

In the image above, you can see the downsides of this full library approach. Montmorillonite and calcite are likely really in the core. Elemental sulfur is obviously nonsense, and all of the feldspars (which have no diagnostic features in SWIR) are unlikely to be actually recorded in SWIR data.
So, a winner-takes-all approach is really only as good as the pool of potential winners it is exposed to.










Box 1: Pearson correlation against the full library (left) and a curated collection of five minerals (right)


Against the full library, Box 1 is mapped with a host of minerals that have no business being in SWIR data: quartz (no SWIR features at all), Johannsenite (just… probably not) and a whole suite of feldspars. Over 300 different library exemplars won at least one pixel.
Against a curated collection of five common rock-forming minerals, each with diagnostic SWIR features, the map is clean and geologically plausible. It also has gaps, where no exemplar cleared the threshold.







Box 2: Pearson correlation against the full library (left) and the curated collection (right)


Box 2 follows the same pattern, but here the gaps are far bigger. Whole pieces of core go unclassified.
Mapping against a full library sets the method up to fail. Pearson and SAM both compare the entire spectrum and reduce the comparison to a single number. Once a feldspar spectrum is cropped, resampled to the scanner’s wavelengths and continuum-removed, it has nothing diagnostic left, just broad shape and noise. A noisy or featureless pixel can match that very well. The absorption features you actually care about end up competing with the flat, noisy parts of your own data.
Curating the collection fixes this, and it has real value. You usually know the geology of your core already; what you want from the map is where those minerals are. A curated map shows that clearly.
But curating moves mineral mapping away from being data-driven and towards being knowledge-driven. You will only ever get confirmation of the minerals you expected.
There won’t be any surprises, only gaps.



So, performance can be improved by only presenting the algorithm with a limited selection of exemplars to choose from. It can also potentially be improved by only presenting the algorithm with a limited spectral range to match.







Box 1: Pearson correlation against the full library at 2000–2600 nm (left), the curated collection at 2000–2600 nm (centre) and the curated collection over the full range (right)


Here the spectral range that was used was 2000nm - 2600nm, and by using this range we have selected a spectral region where actual features are more likely to impact the correlation, more than flat noisy regions.
The performance is definitely improved for full library-restricted spectra compared to the full library-full spectra above. There are far fewer matches against spectrally inactive minerals, but there are still a lot of unlikely minerals scoring highly.
The performance of the curated set in restricted range is also very interesting. The legends show the pixel counts, and more pixels are classified overall on the restricted range image, but the gaps are more coherent - the confident Montmorillonite domain from the full-range curated set is largely gone. Montmorillonite and illite share an Al-OH feature near 2200 nm; the main thing separating them in the SWIR is the water feature near 1900 nm, which is much deeper in montmorillonite. Cut the range at 2000 nm and the strongest evidence for montmorillonite goes with it. So the full-range montmorillonite call was driven by water. That might be real smectite, or it might just be water.







Box 2: Pearson correlation against the full library at 2000–2600 nm (left), the curated collection at 2000–2600 nm (centre) and the curated collection over the full range (right)


Again, we see the same improvement in the use of the full library, but here the unlikely minerals are taking a greater proportion of the pixels. Sodalite and strontianite between them account for over a third of the classified core, and are unlikely.
The curated set shows the same montmorillonite-to-illite swap, and it is even starker, montmorillonite is barely present. But here the restricted range also classifies far more of the core. The gaps in the full-range map were not “nothing there”. The Al-OH and carbonate features near 2200 and 2340 nm were present all along, but outside that window the spectra didn’t look enough like any exemplar, and the whole-spectrum correlation fell below the threshold. By restricting the range to where the features are, the features have a much greater impact on the match.
This approach also raises a potential issue with the default threshold; a correlation of 0.7 over a restricted 600 nm range is not the same test as 0.7 over the full range, so the threshold changes meaning when the range does.
This has demonstrated that mineral mapping is not a final product, but something to be interpreted.
To really get the most out of them, you have to put your thumb on the scale. You need to apply domain knowledge of:

The likely mineralogy of what you are looking at;
The spectral features you expect from that mineralogy, and where they are;
What the applicable threshold should be.

When I first started looking into spectral geology, I thought mineral maps were a data-driven product. They look and smell data-driven.
However, to get a mineral map that is useful, it ends up looking like a knowledge-driven product after all.
With all the caveats from above that this may not apply to every mineral map product that you might have seen

title: Tetra-CORE-der
text:
Expert systems
(These don’t alliterate as cleanly.)
I am going to look at two expert systems, of many. Both are published, and both are purely knowledge-driven: no library matching and no correlation, just actual measurements from the spectra and tested by thresholds that someone who knows the minerals has chosen.
Before the figures, a caveat that applies to both. These are not fair tests. A decision tree is built for a particular geology, and its thresholds encode what the author expected to find there. Below, I run each tree on core it was not built for, as-is, with no tuning. That is the point I want to make, but it means the maps show what happens when a tree is moved, not how well it works at home. Additionally, the HypPy algorithm was ran using HypPy, but on a decision tree that I coded from descriptions in the paper - mistakes in implementation and performance are entirely my own and do not reflect on the authors’ work.

HypPy system
Taken from van Ruitenbeek, F.J.A., Bakker, W.H., van der Werff, H.M.A., Hecker, C.A., Hein, K.A.A. and van Eijndthoven, W. (2025): A Knowledge-Based Strategy for Interpretation of SWIR Hyperspectral Images of Rocks; Remote Sensing, 17(15), 2555.







The interpretation strategy, after van Ruitenbeek et al. (2025)


This paper is a response to several of the problems I raised above, among others (read it, it is very good). Their answer is to classify on the wavelength positions of absorption features, which are set by the physics of the mineral and do not change between scenes. Each pixel gets the position and depth of its three deepest features, and decision trees with fixed thresholds turn those into classes.
Note that the decision tree is step 1 of 5. The strategy is to explore the results, compare them with petrography and chemistry, then build a tree specific to the rocks in hand, and only then run it as a processing chain.







Box 1: the HypPy 2100–2400 nm decision tree


About 70% of this box lands in one of the “other” classes. Those are pixels with a perfectly real deepest feature, in a position the tree has no mineral for. The largest class, at 30%, is a deepest feature between 2220 and 2240 nm. Montmorillonite has nowhere to go either: an Al-OH feature near 2205 nm with no partner near 2350 nm falls through the white mica test into “other 2180–2220”. Meanwhile serpentine, amphibole/talc, epidote/chlorite and prehnite all appear, because this tree was written for hydrothermally altered volcanics from the Pilbara.
None of this is a failure of the method. It is the method telling you that it does not know this rock, which is arguably better than a confident wrong answer. But it does show that a decision tree is only as portable as its author’s experience.


Carbonate spectral facies
Taken from Rogers, R. and Pracht, M. (2023): Hyperspectral Facies Analysis as a Lithological Interpretation Tool for Carbonate Rocks; Geosciences, 13(12), 381.
Yes, this is my paper, but I already had the code.







The carbonate facies decision tree, after Rogers and Pracht (2023)


This tree is much simpler. It asks two questions: is there a feature near 2200 nm (argillaceous material, “muddy” or “clean”), and where is the carbonate feature near 2320 nm (calcite to dolomite, in 10 nm bins)? Ten facies, built for the Irish Carboniferous. The code lives in CoreSpecViewer as an archive, and can be seen here.







Box 2: the carbonate facies decision tree


This is closer to home, Irish Carboniferous carbonate, and the result is far more plausible: muddy and clean calcite dominate, with dolomitic patches and a quenched domain. But it is speckled, and it is not entirely fair to the paper either:

The paper’s facies were read as downhole logs and box-scale patterns, where pixel-scale noise averages out. A single box at pixel resolution shows the noise the logs smoothed over.
The “is there a 2200 nm feature?” test in this archived code accepts any local minimum in the window, with no depth threshold. A little noise in a clean limestone is enough to call it muddy, which will be inflating the muddy facies here. (I wrote that, and I’d add a depth threshold today.)
Every pixel with a carbonate feature is forced into one of eight bins. The tree cannot say “not carbonate” except through the quenched classes, so anything else is reported as a carbonate facies.

The pattern is the same as with the curated libraries: the knowledge goes in up front, and you get back what the tree’s author expected. Inside the workflow that they were specifically designed for, they can produce very useful products. Outside of that specific workflow, they need customising, and in HypPy’s case that customising is built into the method.

title: Tetra-CORE-der
text:
Tetracorder, splitting the difference
(You got your library in my decision tree!)
So, we have looked at two approaches. Correlation methods compare whole spectra against a library and give you a number but no reason. Decision trees measure features and give you reasons, but only the ones their authors included.
Tetracorder, built by Roger Clark and colleagues at the USGS over decades, is both. It is a decision tree whose leaves are library comparisons.
Roger N. Clark, Gregg A. Swayze, K. Eric Livo, Raymond F. Kokaly, Steve J. Sutley, J. Brad Dalton, Robert R. McDougal and Carol A. Gent, 2003, Imaging spectroscopy: Earth and planetary remote sensing with the USGS Tetracorder and expert systems, Journal of Geophysical Research, Vol 108.
Authoritative repo

Tetracorder overview
This is a very high level overview; read the paper for all the details (it is very good).
Tetracorder runs on Linux, is written in Rational Fortran (Ratfor) on top of the USGS specpr package, and is driven by cmd files. Tetracorder-lite builds the original in a Docker container and has a Python interface to drive the cmd files and the original.
I have reconstructed the original cmd files that contained the expert system into a structured json dataset, and have reimplemented the numerical calculation modules from the original system into Python. I felt the need to do this because the expert system is the valuable part, and in its native form it is very hard to get at. The rules are spread across cmd files, with thresholds substituted in from preset files at run time, so you can’t easily see what a rule actually tests for, let alone change it. Running the original means running a Linux build of a 30-year-old Fortran system, one pixel at a time, configured for airborne and orbital sensors. I wanted to point it at core scanner data, switch off the parts that make no sense for core, see why a rule won or lost, and plug it into CoreSpecViewer. That meant reimplementing it, and that only counts if the port gives the same answers as the original, which it mostly does (fidelity work).
I am going to define some terminology to discuss Tetracorder, although a lot of this terminology is my own mental shorthand.







Term
Description




Rule
Contains a library reference spectrum, the features to be tested and constraints it must conform to.


Feature
Can be a positive or NOT feature.


Positive feature
A wavelength interval bounded by two continuum windows, and tests it must pass.


NOT feature
Points to a feature of another rule. If that feature is present above a set depth and fit, this rule is rejected.


Role
Each positive feature has a role; diagnostic, must-have, weak or optional. Diagnostic and must-have features count towards the fit and must be present; weak features must be present but don’t count towards the fit; optional features count if present and are ignored if absent.


Constraint
Thresholds on the rule’s combined fit, depth or fit × depth, applied on the full rule result after all features have been evaluated.


Fit
An output of the fully evaluated rule. Fit describes how well the target spectrum matches the reference across all of the rule’s features: each feature’s match is weighted by that feature’s size and the results are combined.


Depth
An output of the fully evaluated rule. Depth describes how strongly the reference’s absorptions show up in the target: each feature’s band depth is weighted by that feature’s size and the results are combined.


FD
An output of the fully evaluated rule. Fit × Depth, calculated for each feature and combined the same way.


Group
A collection of rules that compete to obtain the classified material. Only the best fit in a group survives, and competition is generally only within a group


Group 0
Rules that compete in every group, with some exceptions


Case
Certain rules trigger a Case if they win their Group. A Case is a second, smaller competition that only runs when it is triggered, and it refines the winner




A rule
{
  "calcite.33+kaol.33+mus-AMXr2": {
    "kind": "group",
    "number": 2,
    "use": true,
    "udata": "reflectance",
    "convolve": false,
    "preratio": null,
    "preprocess": null,
    "algorithm": "tricorder-primary",
    "id": "calcite.33+kaol.33+mus-AMXr2",
    "library_records": {
      "SMALL": {"library": "[sprlb06]", "record": "1038"}
    },
    "reference_title": "Calcite.33+Kaol.33+Mus AMXr2 W1R1Ba",
    "output_title": "Calcite.33+Kaol.33+Mus AMXr2",
    "materials": [
      {"name": "calcite"},
      {"name": "kaolinite"},
      {"name": "muscovite"}
    ],
    "identification_confidence": 8,
    "constraints": [
      {"test": "FD-FIT>", "values": "[GLBLFDFIT]"},
      {"test": "DEPTH-FIT>", "values": "[GLBLDPFITg2]"},
      {"test": "FITALL>", "values": "[GLBLFITALL]"}
    ],
    "features": ["... truncated ..."]
  }
}


A positive feature
{
  "id": "f1a",
  "number": 1,
  "reference_alias": "a",
  "role": "diagnostic",
  "source_code": "DLw",
  "continuum": "linear",
  "coordinates": "wavelength",
  "windows": [
    [2.135, 2.163],
    [2.235, 2.265]
  ],
  "tests": [
    {"test": "ct", "values": ["[CTHRESH4]"]},
    {"test": "r*bd>", "values": ["[RBD22]"]}
  ]
}


A NOT feature
{
  "id": "n1a",
  "number": 1,
  "reference_alias": "a",
  "role": "not",
  "source_reference": "[NOTMUSCOVITE1]",
  "source_feature": "f2a",
  "depth_condition": {
    "mode": "relative",
    "threshold": 0.22,
    "relative_to_feature": "f1a"
  },
  "fit_threshold": 0.6,
  "source_material": "muscovite-medhigh-Al"
}
I won’t go into the details of the above, but you can see that a rule has a pointer to its library reference spectrum, the materials it represents, a confidence level, its constraints and its list of features. A positive feature has its role, the type of continuum, its two continuum windows and the tests it must pass. A NOT feature has the rule and feature it points to, and the depth and fit that feature must exceed to veto this rule. Values in square brackets, like [GLBLFDFIT], are placeholders filled in from a preset at run time, which is how one rule set is tuned for different sensors.
All of the information required to evaluate each feature, fully evaluate the rule and ultimately classify the pixel is encoded into each rule as a recipe. The evaluation code just follows the recipe, runs the competition, and classifies the pixel with the winning rule id in each group.


The competition and classification
The decision tree element is actually a competition between the final fit value of each fully evaluated rule, within a group.
The fit value that each of the 707 rules has after evaluation is an expression of tremendous domain expertise:

which features are diagnostic, and how much each one counts;
minimum fit and depth thresholds;
NOT features: absorptions that must be absent, so a mineral is rejected if, e.g. a carbonate feature is present where it shouldn’t be;
which spectral region it competes in. Materials compete in groups (1 µm, 2 µm and so on), and each group picks its own best match, so one pixel can have an iron oxide answer and a clay answer.

In other words, it is a curated collection and a restricted spectral range and a decision tree, with the curation done in advance by people who knew far more spectroscopy than I do. This system is mature, has been validated by years of ground truth work and is the standard tool for major data releases (e.g. the EMIT L2B products).
It was, however, built for airborne and planetary data, not core.

title: Tetra-CORE-der
text:
Tetra-CORE-der






Box 1, Tetracorder defaults, no mask







Box 2, Tetracorder defaults, no mask





These two maps are the result of feeding our two boxes directly to Tetracorder, using only the default presets and no masks or custom disabled material list.
Interestingly, amusingly, and perhaps unsurprisingly the algorithm identified the wooden core box of Box 2 as dryveg.wood and the cardboard box of Box 1 as a mixture of dryveg.grass.golden and dry_long_grass-thick. This entertainingly (to me, anyway) demonstrates that there are some remote sensing assumptions built into the machinery that we need to accommodate for core scanning uses.
Refinement one; we are not interested in the box or background composition and we almost certainly have a core mask, let’s use it.






Box 1, masked







Box 2, masked





These are much nicer. Box 1 is showing dolomite as we should expect by now, and Box 2 has large coherent domains of calcite. But perchlorate_mg? In great quantities in both boxes? Probably not.
The perchlorate_mg rule is for the hydrated salt, magnesium perchlorate, and I would guess that it was included in the original rule set because it was found on Mars. Not relevant to core scanning - for the moment.
There are a number of other rules like this, that exist for a circumstance I am not using. Tetracorder itself actually recognises this, and has machinery to declare certain rules as not to be used.
Tetracorder disables materials in three ways;

User declared disabled,
Disabled by temperature and pressure constraints, which are used to stop ice and water rules competing in desert scenes,
Disabled by the limitations of the instrument’s band range.

My Python port also carries this machinery and I have assembled a core scanning disabled materials list with entries like perchlorate_mg, snow, ice, water, and all the vegetation categories.






Box 1, masked, core disabled list







Box 2, masked, core disabled list





Okay, this is starting to look plausible and useful. The vast majority of pixels are classified, and most of those are classified by realistic possibilities. There are a few outlandish classification remaining, but not on the same scale as the options presented by the full library comparisons in the winner-takes-all maps above.
At this level, Tetracorder has a second layer of expertise encoded, in its post-processing. The raw output is one image per rule, and a map with 80 rule ids on it isn’t something anyone wants to log from. So the native system ships with theme scripts (27 of them, written for davinci) that gather rules into colour themes: a 2 µm minerals map, a 1 µm minerals map, water, pyroxenes and so on. It also ships with a classification that groups each rule’s materials into mineral families. This is the step where calcite.ws272.g2 and calcite+dolomite.5 stop being separate answers and become calcite, and calcite + dolomite.
I have emulated this, essentially producing a core scanning theme: a lookup that assigns every rule a core logging category, the names a geologist would actually write on a log. Rules that have no business in a core shed (vegetation, ices, exotic salts) are tagged as non-geo, which is also where most of the disabled list above came from.






Box 1, masked, core disabled list, core look-ups







Box 2, masked, core disabled list, core look-ups





These read like a core log. But be aware of what the lookup is doing: when calcite+0.2Na-mont wins on fit, the map now says “calcite + smectite”. It is not just merging names. It turns “this mixture reference fitted best” into “these minerals are present”, which is a stronger claim than the fit alone supports.
However, this has been the case with every flavour of mineral map that we have looked at.

title: Tetra-CORE-der
text:
Conclusions
Pretty pictures, perilous pitfalls.
Every mineral map in this note looked confident but not all of them deserved to.
We have seen three approaches to mineral mapping.
Whole-spectrum library matching appears data-driven, but without curating the choices or restricting the range it will confidently present geologically implausible results. Introducing expertise into the interpretation is not a problem in itself, but those curation decisions and the thinking behind them are not inherently recorded in the image.
Decision trees have the opposite approach, in these the knowledge and final decisions are all presented clearly up front, they are the whole system. But they are only as comprehensive as the knowledge encoded by their authors. Apply them to unfamiliar geology, and they may miss real minerals, return large unclassified areas, or confidently assign the wrong classes.
Tetracorder combines the strengths of both. The knowledge encoded in it is granular and fantastically detailed, it is run feature by feature, on features an expert chose, with an expert’s rules about what must be present, what must be absent and what competes with what. The curation, the spectral range and the decision tree are all in one place, written down, and in Python they can be read and changed. When it calls perchlorate in a carbonate, you can open the rule and see exactly why.
But Tetracorder is not immune to the same problems. Its rule set was developed for particular applications, instruments and environments. Moving it to core scanning requires choices about masking, excluded materials, instrument constraints and how its outputs should be grouped into geological categories. The post-processing decisions and grouping are not just cosmetic, they are a fundamental part of the interpretation.
There is also an important distinction between identifying a spectral match and identifying a mineral. A spectrum matching a reference mixture does not independently establish the presence of every mineral in that mixture. Converting rule identifiers into convenient geological names can obscure that distinction, just as a colourful winner-takes-all map can obscure a poor correlation.
The product of a mineral mapping effort is not the final product. It is simply something else to be interpreted while trying to solve whatever problem required you to understand your geology. And if you think about a mineral map in that sense, then it is vital that all the decisions, methods, and assumptions that created it are explicit and available.
That is the real case for Tetracorder, and the reason I ported it. The knowledge, decisions and assumptions are up front and explicit (and accessible to a wider audience now it is in json and the Python ecosystem). But it still fundamentally compares pixel spectra against library spectra.
It is not a finished core product. It was built for airborne and planetary scenes, and it shows: it mapped the boxes as wood and grass, and found Martian salts in Irish limestone. Almost every pixel gets an answer, whether or not the answer is strong. And the look-ups that make the result readable also turn “this mixture fitted best” into “these minerals are present”.
So the conclusion is the one van Ruitenbeek et al. build into their method: the mineral map is where interpretation starts. Check it against the core, the petrography and the chemistry, then tune it for the rocks in hand. The difference with Tetracorder is that much of the expertise is already there to start from.

text:
Just like Part 1, this note draws heavily on the expertise of Thiele et al., not just their Benchmark Dataset, but also the methodology from their accompanying paper.
I ended Part 1 with some “Conclusions” or “Hypotheses”. After giving it some thought I have re-worked what I actually want to test:
I have decided not to test Group 1 winners here. Although the benchmark dataset does cover the same range as the Group 1 rules, my data does not, and I want to test Tetracorder for SWIR only instruments.
I will also only perform comparisons on the raw winners Tetracorder produces, not on my post-processing aggregations - these are still preliminary and will hopefully be informed by this work.
And one final caveat: all of the references to Tetracorder results in this note refer to results produced using python-tetracorder and not the authoritative release of Tetracorder. title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 2
text:
Methodology

Anatomy of a python-tetracorder run
Unlike classic Tetracorder, python-tetracorder stores the winners and float values of the winner’s characteristics as ndarrays, rather than streaming 8-bit rasters to disk.
So for some context, here are some of the raw outputs from Tetracorder run 4 - the true SWIR run.
from tetracorderp import GroupEvaluator

# an existing run saved to npz can be re-materialised 
run = GroupEvaluator.from_npz("path/to/run4_sg11-2_g2_trueswir/Geyer_bG16_tetracorder.npz")
print(run.group_winners.keys())
#dict_keys([2]) run.group_winners a dictionary of all of the data for the groups analysed
print(run.group_winners[2].keys())
#dict_keys(['winner', 'fit', 'depth', 'fit_depth'])
winners = run.group_winners[2]["winner"]
fit = run.group_winners[2]["fit"]
depth = run.group_winners[2]["depth"]
fit_depth = run.group_winners[2]["fit_depth"]

print(winners.shape, winners.dtype)
#(31, 45) object

print("Pixel winner: ", winners[15, 23])
print("Winner's fit: ",fit[15, 23])
#Pixel winner:  clinochlore.fe.sc-cca-1
#Winner's fit:  0.9536203







Figure 1. The pixel spectrum and reference spectrum of the Tetracorder winner call.


Tetracorder called this pixel clinochlore.fe.sc-cca-1, a member of the chlorite mineral group. Figure 1 shows the spectrum of the pixel and the spectrum of the winning reference (left), and the spectral windows that this rule assesses on this reference (centre and right).
So, Tetracorder provides a rich dataset, with the classification and the corresponding values for each winner.


Anatomy of an MLA dataset
The MLA data are stored as ENVI files, indexed by the hycore hyShed system. A few of the MLA files don’t open cleanly through hycore, so I read the ENVI files directly with Spectral Python.
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import hycore
from spectral.io import envi

hole_name = "Geyer" 
sample_name = "bG16"

shed_path = Path("path/to/Helmholtz_benchmark/MLA/MLA.shed")

shed = hycore.loadShed(shed_path)
boxes = shed.getBoxes()
box = shed.getHole(hole_name).getBox(sample_name)
mla_path = (shed_path / f"{box.holeName()}.hyc"/ f"{box.name}.hyc" / "MLA_HSI.hdr")
mla_img = envi.open(str(mla_path))
mineral_channels = [n.strip() for n in mla_img.metadata["band names"]]
mla = np.asarray(mla_img.load(), dtype=np.float32).transpose(1, 0, 2)  # ENVI -> hylite (x, y)  
print("mla shape: ", mla.shape)
print("number of mineral channels: ", len(mineral_channels))
#mla shape:  (31, 45, 70)
#number of mineral channels:  70
print(mla[15, 23])
#[0.3669482  0.18056996 0.01277622 ... ...]
print("Most abundant mineral in pixel: ", mineral_channels[np.argmax(mla[15,23])])
#Most abundant mineral in pixel:  Quartz
PRESENT = 0.001                                           # Arbitrary presence threshold
present_mins = {mineral: round(float(ab), 3) for mineral, ab in zip(mineral_channels, mla[15, 23]) if ab > PRESENT}
for mineral, abundance in present_mins.items():
  print(mineral, abundance)
#Quartz 0.398
#Albite 0.248
#K-feldspar 0.332
#Chamosite Chl 0.012
#Muscovite Mica 0.008
#Apatite 0.001







Figure 2. Geyer bG16: Tetracorder Group 2 winners as mineral groups (left), and the most abundant SWIR-active mineral group in the MLA at any abundance (right). The example pixel used in the code blocks is outlined.


In the single pixel code above, Tetracorder decided it was clinochlore.fe.sc-cca-1, while the MLA shows that the pixel is dominated by quartz and feldspar. Tetracorder is never going to report quartz and feldspar - they are simply not active in the SWIR range. So, we need to compare Tetracorder with SWIR-active minerals only (as in Figure 2).
In the example pixel, the SWIR-active minerals in the MLA are chamosite and muscovite - so Tetracorder’s clinochlore is wrong. But is it completely wrong? Well, no, not completely. It has identified the mineral species incorrectly, but it has recognised that there is a chlorite there.


A hierarchy of apples to compare
So, how can you systematically compare a Tetracorder winner of the form clinochlore.fe.sc-cca-1 with MLA channels of the form Chamosite or Muscovite Mica? String matching, partial string matching or regex seem doomed to failure (as well as being no fun at all). We need to define a common vocabulary between the two datasets.
Mineral names come in levels, and neither dataset sticks to one level.
The spectral group is the level that SWIR spectroscopy actually sees. Tetracorder identifies an absorption, the features near 2.25 and 2.33 µm, then names the reference spectrum that best matches it. Getting the spectral group right means Tetracorder found the right kind of absorption. Getting the mineral group right means it matched the right family of reference spectra. Getting the species right means the fine detail of the feature, such as its exact position as Fe replaces Mg in a chlorite, also lined up.
The spectral group is not a neat layer above the mineral group. Most chlorites absorb at Fe/Mg-OH, but cookeite, a Li-Al chlorite, absorbs at Al-OH. So every species has exactly one mineral group and (for the purposes of this comparison) exactly one spectral group, and the two are treated as separate labels rather than a strict tree.
The MLA reports chamosite and clinochlore as species in some samples, but just “Chlorite” at another. Among the smectites it only reports nontronite. Tetracorder has species-level references, such as clinochlore.fe.sc-cca-1, alongside generic ones like chlorite, and mixtures such as muscovite+chlorite. So every MLA channel and every Tetracorder rule is mapped to all three levels, and a comparison can only be as fine as the coarser of the two sides. A generic “Chlorite” MLA channel can never produce a species match.
Each pixel gets the single finest level at which the two agree:

Species: the same mineral.
Group: a different species in the same mineral group.
Spectral: a different mineral group with the same absorbing bond.
Miss: none of the above.

Tetracorder can also return no winner at all and those are counted separately. A mixture rule counts as a match if any of its components matches.
Back to the example pixel: the MLA’s dominant SWIR-active mineral is chamosite, an Fe chlorite. Tetracorder called an Fe-rich clinochlore, which sits next to chamosite on the same Mg–Fe solid solution. That is a group match. Tetracorder didn’t name the right species, but it found the right absorption and the right mineral family.
So, to compare apples with apples, I need to define the mappings:
Tetracorder winning rule <–> Common species/group/spectral vocabulary <–> MLA channel

Species differ, mineral group agrees, this pixel is a group match.


Constructing the lookups
Tetracorder has 213 rules that can produce a Group 2 result: 200 Group 2 rules, plus 13 case 6 rules that a Group 2 winner can hand over to (the calcite, epidote and chrysotile rules trigger case 6). Each rule lists the material, or materials, its reference spectrum represents, in RULE_LOOKUP_MATERIAL. Every material was assigned a species, mineral group and spectral group by hand. Where a rule’s material is only generic (chlorite, for example), the species is left blank, so that rule can never score a species match.
64 rules are mixtures of two to four materials, such as muscovite+chlorite or prehnite+.75chlorite. Mixtures are kept as one row per component, and a mixture counts as a match if any of its components matches.
The MLA has 121 distinct channel names, pooled over all 204 samples. Many are duplicates created by site naming: chamosite appears as “Chamosite”, “Chamosite Chl” and “FeChlorite”, depending on the site. Each channel was mapped to the same three levels, giving 14 species reported under more than one name. Where a channel only names a group, as “Chlorite” does at one site, its species is left blank. 44 of the 121 channels are SWIR-active (Al-OH, Fe/Mg-OH, CO3 or H2O). The other 77 are SWIR-inactive (quartz, feldspars, sulphides, oxides and so on) or aren’t minerals at all (Porosity, Unknown and Other).

Thiele et al. 2026 lookups
To score Tetracorder the same way the benchmark scores its models, both lookups also carry the paper’s group. These are the 22 mineral groups from the benchmark’s own data preparation notebook (Code/1_DataPrep.ipynb), whose thesaurus merges MLA channels into groups (chloritoid into chlorite, siderite into ankerite, and so on) and ignores Porosity, Unknown, Other and cassiterite. 72 of the 121 MLA channels fall into one of the 22 groups.
On the Tetracorder side, each rule component was assigned whichever of the 22 groups the paper would (presumably) file it under. White micas follow the paper’s split into muscovite, illite and lepidolite, siderite goes to ankerite, and all sulphates go to sulphate. 83 rules name nothing in the 22 groups (smectites, prehnite, serpentine, talc and so on). A pixel won by one of them predicts none of the 22, so in the paper’s scheme it can miss what’s there, but never score a hit or a false positive.
The resulting lookups can be examined:
Tetracorder mapping
MLA mapping
If you feel strongly enough to thoroughly read the lookups, and don’t agree with them, then I really, really want to hear about what I got wrong!


Using the lookups
In code, the two lookups do one job each. The Tetracorder lookup takes a winning rule and returns every species, mineral group and spectral group it names: one row for a single-material rule, several for a mixture. The MLA lookup takes a channel name and returns its single species, mineral group and spectral group. The cell below loads both, then puts the example pixel through them, so the two tables in the previous section are now computed rather than typed.
It also defines match_level, the rule from the previous section in code form: check species, then mineral group, then spectral group, and return the first level at which the winner and the MLA channel agree. A blank on the MLA side, such as the species of a generic “Chlorite” channel, can never match, so a comparison is never finer than its coarser side.
import pandas as pd

SWIR_ACTIVE = {"Al-OH", "Fe/Mg-OH", "CO3", "H2O"}                # spectral groups with a SWIR absorption
VOCAB = ["species", "group", "spectral_group"]                   # the three levels of the common vocabulary

rule_lookup = pd.read_csv("path/to/group2_crosswalk_long.csv", keep_default_na=False)
mla_lookup = pd.read_csv("path/to/mla_channels.csv", keep_default_na=False).set_index("mla_channel")

# Tetracorder side: the example pixel's winner, and everything it names (a mixture names several)
rule = winners[15, 23]
tet_sets = {level: set(rule_lookup.loc[rule_lookup["rule_id"] == rule, level]) - {""} for level in VOCAB}
print(rule, tet_sets)
#clinochlore.fe.sc-cca-1 {'species': {'clinochlore'}, 'group': {'chlorite'}, 'spectral_group': {'Fe/Mg-OH'}}

# MLA side: the example pixel's most abundant SWIR-active channel
pixel = pd.Series(mla[15, 23], index=mineral_channels).fillna(0)
active = pixel[mla_lookup.loc[pixel.index, "spectral_group"].isin(SWIR_ACTIVE)]
channel = active.idxmax()
truth = mla_lookup.loc[channel, VOCAB]
print(channel, round(active.max(), 3), truth.to_dict())
#Chamosite Chl 0.012 {'species': 'chamosite', 'group': 'chlorite', 'spectral_group': 'Fe/Mg-OH'}


# the finest level at which a winner and an MLA channel agree
def match_level(tet_sets, truth):
    for level, name in zip(VOCAB, ["species", "group", "spectral"]):
        if truth[level] != "" and truth[level] in tet_sets[level]:
            return name
    return "miss"


print(match_level(tet_sets, truth))
#group
Different species, same mineral group: the example pixel is a group match, as worked out by hand above.



Tetracorder runs
All runs were made with a single script, Tet_run_script.py, which writes each run to its own folder alongside a run_settings.json recording exactly how it was made.
Every run starts from the same FENIX reflectance cubes, with the first and last 10 bands dropped as noisy (from the pre-processing methodology of Thiele et al.), leaving 412–2448 nm. Pixels with any missing band are masked. Each run then varies one thing:

Smoothing (runs 2 and 3). In Part 1, I suggested that Savitzky–Golay smoothing with a window of 11 and a second-order polynomial suits Tetracorder best, while Thiele et al. used 5 and 1. Runs 2 and 3 differ only in this.
Group 1 (runs 1 and 2). I said at the start that comparisons are confined to Group 2, the group that matters for my own data. But some Group 1 rules act as NOT vetoes on Group 2 rules (calcite is vetoed by a Group 1 chlorite + muscovite reference, for example), and the benchmark’s FENIX data cover Group 1’s range. Run 1 enables Group 1 so its effect on Group 2 can be measured; Group 1’s own results aren’t compared.
True SWIR (run 4). The FENIX covers the VNIR and the SWIR, but a SWIR-only instrument doesn’t. Run 4 uses only the bands from the SWIR detector, which starts at 974 nm. The VNIR bands are passed to Tetracorder as invalid, so any feature or continuum window below 970 nm is out of range, and the smoothing is applied to the SWIR bands only, so the window never straddles the join between the two detectors. Group 2 rules that rely on a VNIR feature, such as siderite’s broad Fe²⁺ absorption, can’t be called. This is the run closest to scanning core with a SWIR camera.
All runs use Tetracorder’s default thresholds (mode="default"), room temperature (288–298 K), and case 6, which a Group 2 winner can hand over to. Group 0 normally competes in Group 2, and it is enabled, but every one of its rules is among the disabled materials below, so it never wins.

Disabled materials
Separately from whole groups, individual rules can be switched off by passing a list of rule ids to the run. The list for these runs comes from core_lookups.json, the lookup I use to map every Tetracorder rule onto a core-logging class. In that lookup, every rule whose reference isn’t a geological material is tagged non-geo: vegetation, liquid water, snow and ice, plastics, paints, fibreglass, hydrocarbons, cyanides and the World Trade Center dust and debris references. Portlandite (cement) and brucite are tagged non-geo too. Brucite is a real mineral, but on core it only ever fitted noise and water-band wiggles. None of these has any business winning on drill core, so all non-geo rules are disabled. While the full use of that particular lookup to classify core is preliminary, I am confident in the classifications of non-geo.
Five more rules are disabled by name. chalcedony and hydrated_basaltic_glass are broad, single-feature references with no NOT vetoes, so they fit almost any broad 2.2 µm or water absorption and win pixels they have no real claim to. They misbehave. azurite.ws316.g2, malachite.hs254.3b.g2 and nontronite.ng-1.a.g2 rely on VNIR features that a SWIR-only instrument can’t see, so they would be judged, poorly, on half their evidence. They are disabled in every run, so the runs differ only in the settings in the table.
A disabled rule is never evaluated, so any NOT veto that uses it never fires. This is native Tetracorder behaviour, and here it’s what I want. 44 Group 2 rules carry a veto sourced from a non-geo rule, almost all from white_pvc_pipe, dryveg.grass.long or vegetation1, including the whole chlorite, amphibole, serpentine and talc families. Those vetoes exist to stop Mg-OH rules winning on plastic and dry vegetation. Drill core carries neither, so on core any of those vetoes firing could only be a false veto.

title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 2
text:
Hypothesis testing
We have now defined what a Tetracorder run looks like, what the MLA data look like, and a common vocabulary to compare the two. All that remains is to actually compare them.
Each hypothesis is tested below on the example sample, Geyer bG16. (The full single sample example can be run from this script). The cells pick up the winners, fit, depth, mla and mineral_channels loaded earlier. Every comparison is made pixel by pixel. A pixel is used if the MLA has data there and it isn’t entirely porosity, unknown or other (those three together under 70%).
The same operations were then run over all 204 samples and every Tetracorder run, using this code, and those results are in the next section.

H1: is Group 2’s winner the most abundant SWIR-active mineral?
For each pixel, I take the most abundant SWIR-active MLA channel (the dominant mineral in the code block) and compare it with Tetracorder’s winner, using the lookups to put both into the common vocabulary. This is the most abundant channel, not the most abundant mineral group. Channels are what carry the species, so species matches need them. The cost is that a pixel with 8% chamosite and 7% clinochlore holds 15% chlorite, yet no single channel reaches the 10% threshold below, so the pixel isn’t counted. Each pixel gets the finest level at which the two agree:

Species: the winner names the same mineral species as the dominant mineral. For example, the MLA’s dominant mineral is clinochlore and Tetracorder’s winner is a clinochlore reference.
Group: the species differ, but both are in the same mineral group. For example, the MLA says chamosite and Tetracorder says clinochlore: both chlorites.
Spectral: the mineral groups differ, but both absorb through the same bond, so Tetracorder found the right kind of absorption but named the wrong mineral. For example, the MLA says amphibole and Tetracorder says chlorite: both Fe/Mg-OH.
Miss: the winner and the dominant mineral don’t agree at any level.
No call: Tetracorder has no winner for the pixel.

Each level only counts its own pixels, so a species match isn’t also counted as a group match. A comparison can be no finer than the coarser side: if the MLA channel only names a group (e.g. just “Chlorite”), a pixel can match at group level at best. A mixture rule matches if any of its components does. To keep this about minerals that are actually there in quantity, only pixels where the dominant mineral makes up at least 10% are counted.
That gives a breakdown of how Tetracorder does on each MLA mineral group, but it only looks one way. It shows how often Tetracorder gets chlorite pixels right, not how often it says chlorite when there isn’t any. For that, each mineral group is scored as a yes/no question on every pixel: did Tetracorder call chlorite, and is chlorite the dominant SWIR-active group? From that come:

Precision: when Tetracorder calls chlorite, how often is it right?
Recall: of the chlorite-dominated pixels, how many did Tetracorder call chlorite?
MCC (Matthews correlation coefficient): a single score from −1 to 1 that uses all four outcomes, with 0 meaning no better than chance. It’s the metric Thiele et al. use, and it isn’t flattered by rare classes the way accuracy is.

A mixture rule counts as a call for every mineral group it contains.
Each group is only scored in samples where the MLA reports it, so a site that doesn’t distinguish a mineral isn’t counted as a site where it’s absent.
Step by step, the cell below:

Marks which MLA channels are SWIR-active, which are porosity, unknown or other, and which mineral group each channel belongs to.
For each pixel, skips it if there’s no MLA data or it’s mostly porosity, unknown or other.
Finds the dominant mineral: the most abundant SWIR-active channel, if it makes up at least 10%.
Looks up everything Tetracorder’s winner names, at every level.
Scores the winner against the dominant mineral at the finest level they agree, or records no call.
Counts the match levels, then asks the yes/no question for each mineral group to get precision, recall and MCC.







NoteCode: H1 on the example sample. Expand to read dense code block





#%% H1: Is Group 2's winner the most abundant SWIR-active mineral?
MIN_DOMINANT = 0.10                                               # dominant SWIR-active mineral must be at least 10%
EXCLUDE = ["Other", "Unknown", "Porosity"]

active_mask = mla_lookup.loc[mineral_channels, "spectral_group"].isin(SWIR_ACTIVE).to_numpy()
exclude_mask = np.isin(mineral_channels, EXCLUDE)
channel_group = mla_lookup.loc[mineral_channels, "group"].to_numpy()

rows = []
for x, y in np.ndindex(winners.shape):
    abundances = np.nan_to_num(mla[x, y])
    if abundances.sum() == 0 or abundances[exclude_mask].sum() > 0.7:
        continue                                        # no MLA data, or more than 70% Porosity, Unknown, Other

    # MLA side: the most abundant SWIR-active channel, and its mineral group
    active = np.where(active_mask, abundances, 0)
    dominant = mineral_channels[active.argmax()] if active.max() >= MIN_DOMINANT else ""

    # Tetracorder side: the winner and everything it names (a mixture names several)
    rule = winners[x, y]
    tet = rule_lookup[rule_lookup["rule_id"] == rule]
    tet_sets = {level: set(tet[level]) - {""} for level in VOCAB}

    # match level: the finest level at which the winner agrees with the dominant mineral
    if not dominant:
        match = ""
    elif not rule:
        match = "no call"
    else:
        match = match_level(tet_sets, mla_lookup.loc[dominant, VOCAB])

    rows.append({"winner": rule,
                 "dominant": dominant,
                 "dominant_group": channel_group[active.argmax()] if dominant else "",
                 "called_groups": tet_sets["group"], "match": match})

sample = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# match levels, for pixels with a dominant SWIR-active mineral
print(sample.loc[sample["dominant"] != "", "match"].value_counts())
#match
#no call     349
#spectral      2
#Name: count, dtype: int64

# yes/no per mineral group, over every pixel: did Tetracorder call it, and is it the dominant SWIR-active group?
reported = sorted({channel_group[i] for i in np.flatnonzero(active_mask) if np.isfinite(mla[..., i]).any()})
for g in [g for g in reported if (sample["dominant_group"] == g).any()
          or sample["called_groups"].apply(lambda s: g in s).any()]:   # only groups this sample's MLA reports
    called = sample["called_groups"].apply(lambda s: g in s)
    truth = sample["dominant_group"] == g
    tp, fp = (called & truth).sum(), (called & ~truth).sum()
    fn, tn = (~called & truth).sum(), (~called & ~truth).sum()
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else np.nan            # when Tetracorder calls g, how often is it right?
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else np.nan               # of the g-dominated pixels, how many did it call g?
    denom = np.sqrt(float(tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn))
    mcc = (tp * tn - fp * fn) / denom if denom else np.nan       # -1 to 1, 0 = no better than chance
    print(f"{g:12s} n={tp + fn:4d}  precision={precision:.2f}  recall={recall:.2f}  MCC={mcc:.2f}")

H2: Tetracorder detects SWIR-active minerals reliably

H2a: does Tetracorder detect SWIR-active minerals at low abundance in a spectrally neutral matrix?
H1 only asks about the dominant SWIR-active mineral. H2a asks the opposite question: when a SWIR-active mineral is present in small amounts, and nothing else in the pixel absorbs in the SWIR, does Tetracorder find it?
“Nothing else absorbs” needs a definition. I call a pixel a spectrally neutral matrix for a mineral group if every other SWIR-active mineral in it adds up to less than 1%. The rest is quartz, feldspar and other minerals with no SWIR features. In those pixels, the mineral being tested is the only one the MLA reports with a SWIR feature in any quantity. That’s a mineralogical definition, not a spectral one: grain size, scattering and minerals the MLA doesn’t report can still shape the spectrum.
Abundance is split into bins (0–1%, 1–2.5%, 2.5–5%, 5–10%, 10–25% and over 25%), and for each bin I count how often Tetracorder named the mineral group: the detection rate. One extra bin, absent, holds the neutral pixels where the mineral group isn’t there at all. The detection rate in that bin is the false call rate: how often Tetracorder names a mineral that isn’t in the pixel. Without it, a high detection rate could just mean the mineral gets called everywhere.

H2b: is the mineral Tetracorder names actually there?
H1 scored a call as wrong whenever the named mineral wasn’t the dominant one, even if it may have been present at low abundance. H2a suggested that many of those calls are real detections, but on a very specific set of requirements. H2b turns the question round: for every call Tetracorder makes, is the mineral it names present in the pixel at all, whatever its abundance and whatever else is there?
Each call is checked against the MLA at the mineral group level. A mixture rule names several groups, and each is checked separately, so a muscovite + chlorite call asks both whether white mica is there and whether chlorite is there. A named group can be:

Present: the MLA has some of it in the pixel. I also report the stricter present at 1% or more, because the MLA’s smallest values are probably close to its noise.
Absent: the MLA reports that group in this sample, but none of it in this pixel. That’s an unconfirmed call: the MLA measures that group here and found none.
Not reported: the MLA doesn’t measure that group in this sample (alunite, jarosite or prehnite, for example). The MLA can neither confirm nor deny those calls, so they’re counted separately rather than as wrong.

All three are judged against the minerals the MLA reports, which makes this an operational truth, not an absolute one. A mineral group having a channel doesn’t guarantee the MLA picks up trace amounts of it, and smectite shows the asymmetry: the MLA’s only smectite is nontronite, while Tetracorder’s smectite references are mostly Al-OH smectites. Both map to the same group.

H3: do Tetracorder’s metrics track mineral abundance?
Tetracorder reports three numbers for each winner: the fit, how closely the shape of the absorption matches the reference spectrum; the depth, how strong the absorption is; and fit × depth. H3 asks whether any of them rises with how much of the mineral is actually there. If one does, it could stand in for abundance, which Tetracorder doesn’t otherwise report.
This test works at the mineral group level. For each call, the abundance it’s compared with is the MLA’s total for the group the winner names, added up over every channel in that group. A clinochlore winner on a pixel with 3% chamosite and 2% clinochlore is a chlorite call on 5% chlorite. Unlike H1, species-level matches aren’t counted separately; they’re counted along with the rest of their group, and the species detail is set aside. Depth responds to how much of the absorbing bond is there, and chamosite and clinochlore absorb through the same Fe/Mg-OH bond, just slightly shifted. Species abundances would also be fragile, because chlorite almost never matches at species level.
The test only uses correct calls: pixels where the winner names a single mineral group and the MLA says that group is present, at any abundance. A wrong call or no call has no meaningful abundance to compare against. Mixtures are left out, because it isn’t clear which component’s abundance the fit should track. Note this is a selected population: low-abundance pixels are the most likely to be missed altogether, and missed pixels never enter this test. So H3 asks whether fit and depth track abundance where Tetracorder has already recognised the mineral, not whether they could estimate abundance in any pixel.
The relationship is measured with Spearman correlation: a score from −1 to 1, where 1 means the fit (or depth) always rises as abundance rises, and 0 means they’re unrelated. It only asks whether one goes up with the other, not whether they follow a straight line. As a more readable version, the cell also prints the median fit, depth and fit × depth in each of the abundance bins from H2a.

Thiele et al. vocabulary tests
The benchmark models were trained and scored on the paper’s 22 mineral groups. For a direct comparison, I score Tetracorder the same way, reproducing their set-up from the benchmark notebooks:

Only the 61 test sections, the same ones the models never saw in training.
The same pixel mask, as far as the data allow: a 2 × 2 erosion at section edges (MLAStack’s clip=2), and pixels dropped where the 22 groups sum to less than 70%, with the rest renormalised to 100%.
Occurrence: a group is present in a pixel if its abundance is over 2.5%. This is the MCC in their published metrics.
Dominant phase: the most abundant of all 22 groups, quartz and feldspar included.

That leaves 52,722 test pixels, against the paper’s 50,146, about 5% more. The erosion is the same as the benchmark’s (the same function, with the same 2 × 2 element), so the difference isn’t at the section edges. It comes from two steps I couldn’t reproduce. The benchmark code intersects each section with its own mask band before eroding, and I couldn’t use that band (some loading issues). Its stacking code may also drop pixels without valid spectra in the other sensors (FX50, LWIR), which this comparison doesn’t use. So these scores are on a slightly larger set of pixels than the published ones, and I don’t know whether the extra pixels help or hurt Tetracorder.
These scores aren’t a SWIR-only test. Tetracorder can’t call quartz or feldspar, so whenever they dominate, its call can only be a false positive in the dominant-phase score. And any of its 83 rules that name nothing in the 22 groups can only score as a miss. That’s the price of using the benchmark’s own yardstick, and it’s why both sets of tests are reported.
The full Thiele et al. vocabulary comparison can be run using this script.

Builds the two truths: occurrence (every group over 2.5%) and dominant phase (the single most abundant group).
Looks up which of the 22 groups Tetracorder’s winner names. Most rules name one, mixtures several, and some none.
Asks the yes/no question for each group against each truth, giving precision, recall and MCC.

inside = binary_erosion((filled > 0).any(axis=-1), np.ones((CLIP, CLIP)))
total = paper_abundance.sum(axis=-1)
keep = inside & (total >= CLOSURE)
paper_abundance = paper_abundance[keep] / total[keep, None]
print(f"{keep.sum()} of {keep.size} pixels kept")
# 958 of 1395 pixels kept

# the two truths: every group over 2.5% (occurrence), and the single most abundant of all 22 (dominant phase)
occurrence = paper_abundance > OCCURRENCE
dominant = paper_abundance.argmax(axis=1)

# Tetracorder side: which of the 22 groups the winner names (a mixture names several; many rules name none)
rule_paper = {rule: set(groups) - {""} for rule, groups in rule_lookup.groupby("rule_id")["paper_group"]}
called = np.array([[pg in rule_paper.get(rule, set()) for pg in PAPER22] for rule in winners[keep]])

# yes/no per group, against each truth: precision, recall and MCC as in H1
for i, pg in enumerate(PAPER22):
    if not (occurrence[:, i].any() or called[:, i].any()):
        continue                                                  # never present and never called
    result = f"{pg:12s}"
    for name, truth in [("occurrence", occurrence[:, i]), ("dominant", dominant == i)]:
        c = called[:, i]
        tp, fp = (c & truth).sum(), (c & ~truth).sum()
        fn, tn = (~c & truth).sum(), (~c & ~truth).sum()
        precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else np.nan
        recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else np.nan
        denom = np.sqrt(float(tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn))
        mcc = (tp * tn - fp * fn) / denom if denom else np.nan
        result += f"  {name}: n={tp + fn:4d} precision={precision:.2f} recall={recall:.2f} MCC={mcc:.2f}"
    print(result)

Two sets of numbers answer different questions, and any comparison with the trained models has to be read with that in mind.

title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 2
text:
Discussion

What Tetracorder gets right
For white mica, chlorite, calcite or dolomite, Tetracorder is very good. When one of those wins, the MLA confirms its presence 95-99% of the time. Even when the pixel is dominated by SWIR-inactive minerals, Tetracorder often finds a few percent of chlorite or white mica: about half the time at 1–2.5% for chlorite, and two times in three for white mica.
Much of what H1 counted as wrong turns out to be exactly this: correct detections of minerals present at a few percent, in pixels where something else is more abundant. For alteration mapping, where the interesting mineral is often the minor one, that matters more than getting the dominant mineral right.
It also, mostly, fails safe. Tetracorder is reticent to name a mineral unless it is very confident; for the carbonates, no calls outnumber misses by about two to one. For an unsupervised method that is the desired behaviour.
And it does all of this on the SWIR alone, with no training, no site calibration, and default settings. Dropping the VNIR bands cost one mineral (siderite) and slightly improved calcite. Enabling Group 1 changed nothing. Changing the smoothing barely mattered. The results are robust to the settings I tried.


What it gets wrong
Three groups of minerals are a problem, each for a different reason.
Fe/Mg silicates other than chlorite. Amphibole and epidote are almost never named. Tetracorder finds their Fe/Mg-OH absorption and calls it chlorite, or prehnite + chlorite. This isn’t a failure to detect anything; it’s a failure to tell similar features apart, which comes down to the reference library and the rules. In a skarn, or any mafic-hosted system, Tetracorder will report chlorite where the rock is full of amphibole and epidote.
Biotite is invisible: no call in 84% of the pixels where it’s the dominant SWIR-active mineral, and never detected even at 5–25% in a clean matrix. Its iron darkens the whole SWIR and flattens the OH features. A biotite-altered porphyry would look, to Tetracorder, much like unaltered rock.
Dark carbonate. Calcite and dolomite are under-called: 22–26% no calls, and only 68–83% detection even in nearly pure carbonate. The worst samples are all from Stonepark, dark fine-grained limestone where the carbonate feature is likely to be shallow. I haven’t shown that the darkness is the cause, but it’s the obvious candidate. And this is a problem for me specifically, working in the Irish Carboniferous.
There are also calls that shouldn’t be trusted on their own. Smectite is confirmed by the MLA in fewer than 40% of its calls, prehnite in 10%, serpentine never. Some of that is the MLA’s blind spots rather than Tetracorder’s errors (the MLA reports no Al-OH smectite at all), but without independent evidence these calls are suspect.
Species is the wrong level for some minerals. Within a solid solution, such as chlorite or white mica, Tetracorder’s choice of reference doesn’t reliably match the MLA’s species. The mineral group is the honest level to report.
A lot of these failures are attributable to the specific use (abuse?) of Tetracorder in this case. Tetracorder spreads mineral identification across its groups, and I’ve only looked at Group 2. This test focussed on SWIR only references and rules and I either ignored or disabled the rules and references that cover the VNIR, which form a large part of the interconnected algorithm. Biotite, amphibole and epidote all have Fe²⁺ absorptions in the VNIR, which is Group 1’s territory, and I don’t use Group 1’s results at all. Scoring Group 2 alone asks Tetracorder to name these minerals without the part of the system designed to see them. I shouldn’t be surprised that when I cut pieces out of it, it doesn’t work as well.


Depth is a relative proxy for abundance
Tetracorder doesn’t report abundance, but its band depth tracks it. Within a mineral group, a deeper feature consistently means more mineral, with Spearman correlations of 0.45–0.66 and median depths that climb steadily across the abundance bins. Fit doesn’t: it measures how well the shape matches the reference, and once a mineral is recognised the shape matches well regardless of how much is there.
So depth can be used as a relative measure: this interval has more white mica than that one. It isn’t a calibration. The spread of abundance at any given depth is wide, and depths can’t be compared between minerals.


Against the trained models
On the benchmark’s own scoring, Tetracorder trails the models trained on this dataset for every mineral group. For the four it does best, it is 0.15–0.25 MCC behind. Tetracorder’s precision for those groups (0.76–0.90) is comparable with the models’. However, it lacks recall: it finds roughly half the occurrences the models find. The H2 results suggest why. A pixel that is mostly quartz and feldspar, with a few percent of mica, is a weak SWIR signal, and Tetracorder declines to call weak signals.
The comparison with the trained models isn’t like for like. I made it because the benchmark’s methodology was clearly laid out, designed for this very dataset, and the fairest yardstick available.
The trained models use the FENIX, FX50 and LWIR data, predict the abundance of every mineral including the ones Tetracorder can’t see, and were trained on these sites. Tetracorder uses the SWIR alone, has never seen this data, and wasn’t designed to estimate abundance. The models are better at the task they were built for. The question for core scanning is whether a method that needs no training data, and runs on any SWIR instrument, is good enough to be useful. On this evidence, for the common SWIR minerals, it is.


The limits of this test
The MLA is an operational truth. It’s the best mineralogy available at this scale (and public), but it has its own blind spots (no Al-OH smectite, no alunite, no pyrophyllite), its own detection limits, and its own registration to the hyperspectral pixels. Some of Tetracorder’s “false” calls may be real, and some of its “correct” ones may be lucky.
The lookups are my judgement. Every Tetracorder rule and every MLA channel was mapped to the common vocabulary by hand. The lookups are published so they can be checked, but different choices, for illite or chloritoid say, would move some numbers.
One benchmark, seven sites. Rock types and alteration styles the benchmark doesn’t cover may (will!) behave differently, and the per-site differences (Stonepark’s carbonates, for one) show how much the rock matters.
This is python-tetracorder. These results come from my Python port of Tetracorder, run with its default thresholds. The port follows the native code closely, but it is not the native code, and the default thresholds were not designed for core.


What does this mean for core scanning?
For core scanning, the practical value of a mineral classification depends on the question being asked.
If the objective is a quantitative mineralogical model of every pixel, including quartz, feldspar and minerals without diagnostic SWIR features, Tetracorder is not the right tool by itself. The benchmark’s trained models, and the underlying methodology, are demonstrably better suited to that task.
If the objective is to identify the distribution of spectrally active alteration minerals, the results are considerably more favourable. White mica and chlorite can be detected at relatively low abundance, and their positive classifications generally correspond to minerals reported by the MLA. That is useful information even when those minerals represent only a small fraction of the rock.
The principal caution is that a missing classification is not evidence that the mineral is absent. Detection sensitivity differs strongly between minerals, and even abundant carbonates may receive no call. Equally, positive identifications of less reliable groups need more scrutiny than those of white mica, chlorite or the carbonates.
There are practical advantages to the rule-based approach. The rules are inspectable, the reference materials are identifiable, and the system does not require a training dataset representative of every new lithology or geological setting. For surveys and other organisations processing large volumes of varied core, those properties have value. They do not guarantee that a classification will transfer correctly to unfamiliar geology, but they make its assumptions available for examination and its failures open to investigation.
There is also scope for improvement. The experiments identify particular minerals and rules that deserve attention, rather than requiring the entire system to be reconsidered. A core-specific configuration, improved reference selection or more discriminating rules could address some of the observed confusions. Whether those changes actually improve performance would, of course, need to be tested rather than assumed.


What could be improved
Most of the failures can be traced to specific rules, which means they can be fixed in a transparent way. Siderite’s reliance on a 1 µm feature, the vetoes on the calcite rules, and the reference spectra for chlorite, amphibole and epidote are all candidates. A core-specific configuration, improved reference selection or more discriminating rules could address some of the observed confusions. If, and how, those changes actually improve performance would, of course, need to be tested rather than assumed.
Tuning the rules on this benchmark and then testing them on the same benchmark would no longer be testing Tetracorder. It would be fitting it. That needs a held-out test set, and is work for another day.

title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 2
text:
Conclusion
So how good is Tetracorder for core? Good enough. Probably. For some things.

title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 1
text:
One of the difficulties with producing hyperspectral mineral maps is knowing whether they are right. We can make maps that look geologically plausible, but testing the actual mineral identifications requires independent mineralogical data.
Fortunately, Thiele et al. (2026) have published exactly the sort of dataset we need.
Their work combines Mineral Liberation Analysis (MLA) with co-registered hyperspectral imagery from 206 rock samples, covering a wide variety of geological settings. The hyperspectral data span the VNIR, SWIR, MWIR and LWIR, and the MLA provides independent measurements of the mineral assemblages.
The authors use these data to train and benchmark machine-learning methods for predicting quantitative mineralogy from hyperspectral measurements.
I’m interested in something rather different. What happens if we run the hyperspectral data through Tetracorder, using its existing mineral identification rules, and compare the resulting maps with the MLA?
The dataset and associated publication are freely available:
Publication

text:
Tetracorder
I am going to use three samples from the benchmark dataset for illustration during this note (must have images!):



Hole
Sample

bS24


Freiberg
E030B_C12

A little bit of context, taken from Thiele et al (2026):

Collinstown, Zn–Pb prospect in County Westmeath, Ireland, drilled by Teck Ireland. The mineralogical setting includes dolomitisation, hydrothermal alteration and Zn–Pb mineralisation associated with Irish-type deposits.

Freiberg, Germany, drilled by Excellon Resources in 2020. Volcanics, metamorphics and hydrothermal alteration.
Bösenbrunn, Germany, drilled in the 1970s. Volcanics, volcaniclastics, sedimentary clastics and hydrothermal alteration.


Running Tetracorder
The dataset is organised using the hylite ecosystem (hylite, hycore, hyshed). To run Tetracorder on each sample:
from pathlib import Path
import hycore

shed_path = Path("/Path/to/Helmholtz_Benchmark_set/MLA/MLA.shed")
shed = hycore.loadShed(shed_path)

box = shed.get("<hole>").get("<sample>")
The hyperspectral data distributed in the dataset is stored as fractional reflectance with the full band range present and no smoothing. The pre-processing method described in the paper included clipping the first and last 10 bands and smoothing with a Savitzky-Golay algorithm using a first order polynomial with a window size of 5.
To me, this seems like an unusual parameter choice for smoothing (a first-order Savitzky–Golay filter is effectively a moving average) and it may be more appropriate for the ML applications that the dataset was designed for. For Tetracorder, I pre-processed with a second-order polynomial and a window size of 11.
As the Tetracorder rules only cover the VNIR-SWIR range, we will only use the Fenix data from the dataset.
import scipy as sc
import numpy as np

from tetracorderp import GroupEvaluator  

WINDOW = 11
POLY = 2
SLICE = slice(10, -10, None)  

fenix = box.get("FENIX")
identifier = f"{box.holeName()}_{box.name}"

data = fenix.data[..., SLICE]
wavelengths = fenix.get_wavelengths()[SLICE]
fwhm = np.asarray(fenix.header.get_list("fwhm"), dtype=float)[SLICE]  

assert data.shape[-1] == len(wavelengths) == len(fwhm), (
    f"Shape mismatch: data={data.shape[-1]}, "
    f"wavelengths={len(wavelengths)}, fwhm={len(fwhm)}"
)

# Identify spectra with all finite bands - savgol chokes on NaNs
valid_pixels = np.all(np.isfinite(data), axis=-1)

# Allocate output, retaining NaNs for invalid pixels
run_cube = np.full(data.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)

# Smooth only valid spectra
run_cube[valid_pixels] = sc.signal.savgol_filter(data[valid_pixels], WINDOW, POLY, axis=-1)

run = GroupEvaluator(
    run_cube,                                  # The smoothed, pre-processed sample data
    wavelengths / 1000,                        # convert nm to um required by Tetracorder
    fwhm / 1000,                               # convert nm to um required by Tetracorder
    mode="default",                            # Tetracorder's default preset thresholds (this work might lead to a new "core" preset)
    masked_pixels=~valid_pixels,               # mask pixels with NaN                
    temperature=(288, 298),                    # Room temperature in kelvin
    disabled_materials=disabled_materials,     # Core scanning specific disabled list (exclude water, ice, vegetation etc)
    disabled_groups=disabled_groups,           # Core scanning specific disabled list (exclude water, ice, vegetation etc)
    disabled_cases=disabled_cases,             # Core scanning specific disabled list (exclude water, ice, vegetation etc)
)
run.write_npz(OUTDIR / (identifier + f"_tetracorder_run_{WINDOW}_{POLY}.npz")) # persist results for later evaluation
From the results, we can examine what Tetracorder thinks of these samples.
