Initial observations
It is important that I explain the difference between the Tetracorder “Raw winners” and the “Core classifications” shown here. The classifications are lookup-based aggregations of the winning rules, not a second independent analysis. A class such as calcite + dolomite does not necessarily mean that both minerals have been independently identified, just that a spectrum measured from mixed material was the best match.
Additionally the aggregation look-ups are slightly-less-than-arbitrary. I constructed them by grouping rule names and Tetracorder “materials” into minerals and mineral families - as such multiple spectral rules can contribute to the same geological class. This is also what native Tetracorder does with its rules, I have just built a table specific for core.
The first thing to note is that the maps are not random noise. Across all three samples, Tetracorder produces spatially coherent classifications, with identifiable domains and boundaries. This is encouraging, although geological plausibility is only the first hurdle.
Collinstown is particularly interesting. Group 2 is remarkably consistent, identifying almost the entire sample as calcite or calcite + dolomite. Only two spectral rules are responsible for the result. Group 1 identifies a much more diverse assemblage, dominated by Fe²⁺ rules, siderite and amphibole. The two groups are not necessarily contradicting each other: they target different spectral features and can identify different components of the same assemblage.
Freiberg shows a different pattern. Group 1 is dominated by olivine, which seems suspicious, with small regions of other Fe-bearing minerals. Group 2 is more variable, identifying chlorite, calcite, dolomite and associated mineral combinations. The result suggests that Tetracorder is recognising a reasonably consistent alteration assemblage, although we cannot yet say how accurately it represents the measured mineralogy.
Bösenbrunn is rather different again. Group 1 produces a substantial variety of iron-related spectral identifications, particularly those associated with olivine (again, suspicious), iron-bearing minerals and broad Fe²⁺ absorptions. The broader classification map simplifies this into coherent domains dominated by olivine and Fe²⁺-related classes. Group 2, however, is dominated by chlorite, with a small area of chlorite + prehnite.
So, this looks pretty good. We are getting coherent and (bar olivine?) reasonable results across two spectral domains - although Group 2 is “better” than Group 1 in a geological sense.
But is it right? Correct? Accurate? However you want to characterise how much you trust results.
This is precisely why having independent MLA measurements is valuable. The maps look convincing enough, but looking convincing is a very low bar for a mineral classification algorithm.

title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 1
text:
MLA data
The Mineral Liberation Analysis (MLA) provides an independent mineralogical characterisation of each sample.
Unlike the categorical output from Tetracorder, the MLA data are quantitative. Each pixel contains estimated abundances for multiple minerals, rather than a single mineral identification.

Dominant mineral maps
We can represent this information in several ways. The simplest is to assign each pixel the mineral with the highest abundance, producing a dominant mineral map. This provides a useful overview of the mineralogical distribution, but necessarily conceals any other minerals present.






Collinstown MLA dominant mineral







Freiberg MLA dominant mineral







Bösenbrunn MLA dominant mineral





A cursory examination of the dominant mineral maps is encouraging, particularly for Collinstown and Freiberg.
Collinstown is overwhelmingly calcite, with only a few pixels dominated by dolomite or barite. This is consistent with the strong carbonate response in Tetracorder Group 2. The dolomite-dominated pixels at the top of the sample also sit where Group 2 identified calcite + dolomite, although the dominant mineral map does not tell us how much dolomite might be present alongside calcite elsewhere.
Freiberg has a much more varied mineralogy, with substantial areas dominated by plagioclase, chlorite and calcite, alongside smaller areas of quartz and amphibole. The diagonal calcite band follows the carbonate band in Tetracorder Group 2 closely.
Bösenbrunn is dominated by chamosite (an iron-rich chlorite), with small regions of albite and occasional biotite. This is an interesting result given the apparent prevalence of chlorite in Tetracorder Group 2, although Group 1’s iron-related identifications will warrant closer examination.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, olivine is not the dominant mineral in either Freiberg or Bösenbrunn!
Plagioclase and albite dominate large parts of Freiberg and Bösenbrunn, but they have no diagnostic features in the VNIR–SWIR. A pixel that is mostly plagioclase with some chlorite will look like chlorite to Tetracorder, because chlorite is the only thing in it with an absorption to match. Spectral dominance and abundance dominance are not the same thing.
So, these are only dominant mineral maps. They tell us which mineral has the greatest abundance at each pixel. By taking only the dominant mineral we have reduced a quantitative dataset to, effectively, a classification map, discarding what we actually need to test Tetracorder.
The next step is therefore to examine the actual mineral abundances, which are harder to visualise, but that’s where the real test lies.

The calcite + dolomite pixels at the bottom of the sample have no obvious MLA counterpart, so that is one hit and one miss.

In Collinstown, Group 1 found a range of Fe²⁺ responses, but is dominated by two rules: generic.Fe2+nrw.actinolite across the calcite matrix, and siderite1 along a band running down the sample. That band follows the vein where the MLA has barite, pyrite and dolomite, and where calcite abundance drops.
Neither mineral is right as named. There is no actinolite or amphibole channel in the Collinstown MLA, so it was either not present or not set up to be detected. The actinolite rule winning across nearly pure calcite looks like Group 1 fitting weak Fe²⁺ features (perhaps trace Fe in the calcite) to the closest reference it has.
The siderite band is more interesting, because it follows a real mineralogical boundary. There is no siderite channel in the MLA data. Irish-type dolomite can be ferroan, and Fe²⁺ in a carbonate is exactly what a siderite reference would match, so it is tempting to say Group 1 is seeing an Fe-bearing carbonate in the vein. But dolomite is only a small fraction of this sample, and the MLA can’t confirm it. (Freiberg, below, is a cautionary tale about exactly this sort of explanation.)
So Group 1 is separating the matrix from the vein. It is identifying the spatial pattern of the measured mineralogy, even if it is very wrong about the actual minerals.

The upper vein is less clear, but the MLA shows it is quartz-rich (below), and quartz has no VNIR–SWIR features to detect, so the carbonate signal there is diluted rather than missed.
The dolomite is a problem, though: the MLA has no dolomite at all. It does have an ankerite channel however, an Fe-bearing dolomite-group carbonate, which could plausibly sit spectrally between the calcite and dolomite references.

title: So how good is Tetracorder for core? - Part 1
text:
So, how good is it?
On three samples, the honest answer is “better than I expected, in some ways, and for some of the right reasons”.
The SWIR rules (Group 2) found the right spectrally active mineral in all three samples: calcite in Collinstown, chlorite and carbonate in Freiberg, and chlorite in Bösenbrunn. In Collinstown and Freiberg, they also put the carbonate in roughly the right place.
The VNIR Fe rules (Group 1) are much less reliable as mineral identifications. Olivine wins large areas of two samples that contain none, and actinolite wins across a nearly pure calcite. But Group 1 is not useless: its spatial patterns follow real mineralogical boundaries, and in both Collinstown and Freiberg the siderite winners pick out the carbonate veins from the matrix, even though the MLA has essentially no siderite.
Across all three samples, a large fraction of the rock (plagioclase, albite, quartz) is invisible in the VNIR–SWIR. Tetracorder is identifying the minor, spectrally active phases in an otherwise spectrally neutral matrix, and any fair evaluation has to account for that.
Obviously, this is very subjective! All of this looking between mineral maps and comparing spatial patterns is really fun, but what I need is an objective evaluation of Tetracorder’s performance against the full ground-truth dataset. That needs some care: Tetracorder classes have to be mapped onto MLA channels (and some channels, like olivine, don’t exist), the evaluation should be restricted to SWIR-active minerals, and I need to decide how much of a mineral the MLA must report before Tetracorder “should” see it.
Also, I have looked at 3 samples, from a 200+ benchmark dataset. For a blog post.
That’s Part 2. An objective, scientifically rigorous (or close enough for a blog) evaluation against the full benchmark dataset.
Some hypotheses to test (you could call them conclusions from Part 1):

Group 2 correctly identifies the dominant SWIR-active mineral.
Group 1 Fe²⁺ rules over-call olivine and possibly actinolite where the Fe²⁺ actually comes from chlorite or carbonate. This assumes that the absence of an olivine channel in MLA is actually absence of olivine.
Mixed-carbonate classes do not reliably indicate a second carbonate. In Collinstown the calcite + dolomite match partly coincides with real dolomite; in Freiberg there is no dolomite, and mixing with chlorite is a candidate explanation.
Tetracorder detects SWIR-active minerals at low abundance in spectrally neutral matrices. The question is how low.

title: Hyperspectral data is big!
text:
Compared to remote sensing, hyperspectral core scanning produces fairly manageable file sizes.
For a single core box (SWIR data in this example, as that is what I mostly work with):
But there are a lot of them!
A typical project is 10–12 holes of ~80 boxes each, so call it 1000 boxes for a small to medium project. At ~1 GB per box, that is ~1 TB, and the derived data accounts for almost half of it.
But it is derived data. Why not just derive it when you need it?
If you have used CoreSpecViewer, you know that I do store it. All of it, for every box. Here is why.

title: Hyperspectral data is big!
text:
Three strategies
A system working with hyperspectral data has three resources to spend:

Disk
Time
RAM

And there are three ways to handle derived products:

Derive on demand. Compute it when needed, use it, throw it away. Costs time.
Cache in RAM. Compute everything once at startup and hold it. Costs RAM.
Cache to disk. Compute once, store it, read it back. Costs disk.

Let’s go through them, worst first.

title: Hyperspectral data is big!
text:
Cache in RAM
Many of my processes need both the smoothed and the normalised data. We could compute it for a whole hole at startup: a one-time slowdown, then fast iterative work and no wasted disk.
For an 80-box hole at ~300 MB per normalised dataset, that is 24 GB of RAM, before any algorithm allocates a single intermediate array, and before you meet a hole longer than average.
I do not see a >64 GB machine in my professional near future, never mind >128 GB. An 8 GB laptop is probably standard for the average geo-about-town. So this one is out.

title: Hyperspectral data is big!
text:
Derive on demand
This is the option that deserves a proper look. It costs no disk, and its RAM footprint is small, because you only hold one box at a time:



Dataset
Size

~300 MB

~640 MB



Add the intermediates of a feature extraction and you are still under 1 GB. That is nothing, so RAM is not the problem here. Time is.



Derived product
Time




Smoothing
~1–2 s


Continuum removal
~10–30 s



Here is the call signature for feature extraction in CoreSpecViewer:
def Combined_MWL(savgol, savgol_cr, mask, bands, feature, technique='QUAD',
                 use_width=False, cached_arrays=None):
It takes savgol (the smoothed reflectance) and savgol_cr (the normalised reflectance). Mask and bands have to be stored regardless. So, starting from cropped reflectance:



Step

In this straightforward path, caching saves about 40%, which is real, but a slow feature extraction is still slow.
You will never run a feature extraction once. You pick parameters, look at the result, change a threshold, try a different fitting method, look again. You flick between boxes in the viewer, and you build downhole plots. Every one of those is an access.
Derive on demand pays the derivation cost on every access. Caching pays it once, and every access after that costs a disk read.
Ten iterations of tuning across one hole means 800 box accesses. At ~11 s of re-derivation each, that is nearly 2.5 hours spent recomputing data that has not changed. The cached version spends about 13 minutes reading it back. In exploratory, iterative work, the work this software exists for, the number of accesses explodes and the gap explodes with it.

title: Hyperspectral data is big!
text:
So, disk
Disk caching vastly increases the access speed for derived data, but what pushes it over the edge into the absolute preferred option?
Memmapping.
Because everything lives on disk as arrays, CoreSpecViewer can memory-map it. That lets me have a 1 km hole “open” (over 150 GB of data) on an 8 GB RAM machine. Arrays are paged in as they are read and dropped back to the memmap when I am done with them.
You cannot memmap an array that does not exist yet. A whole-hole view built on derive-on-demand would mean deriving the whole hole, which drops us straight back into the RAM problem.
Caching everything looked wasteful when I started, since it nearly doubles the storage. But of the three resources, disk is by far the most abundant and the cheapest. A terabyte costs less than an afternoon of a geologist’s time.
What looked extremely wasteful is actually spending the abundant resource to protect the scarce ones.

title: Hyperspectral data is big!
text:
“Conclusions”…
This conclusion depends on my stack.
“You fool!”, I hear you cry, “you wrote it in Python! Of course it is slow!”
You would not be wrong. Derivation could be pushed into compiled kernels, rewritten in another language, made blazingly fast. If continuum removal took one second instead of ten, the access-count argument would shrink a lot and I would revisit this. Maybe the commercial software world has already solved it. But Python gives me too much (NumPy, SciPy, hylite) for me to move away from it, and with this stack, disk wins.
In a nod to the fact disk caching doubles the storage CoreSpecViewer has an archive file type for long-term storage. This is the minimum dataset needed to deterministically reproduce a fully analysed box. Cache everything while you are working, and archive the minimum when you are done. The rehydrate process is the time penalty up-front when you open an archive, then you are back to working iteratively on memmaps.

title: Hyperspectral core scanning interpretation made easy - sort of!
text:
Hyperspectral core scanning can be daunting for the average geologist. The file types won’t be something you have used before, you may not even recognise them. You will be looking for jpegs or tiffs, but the chances are you will get a directory of many files with .dat, .bil, or .raw extensions.
CoreSpecViewer simplifies this. It ingests multi-file directories directly: Specim Lumo exports, which it was built for, and other acquisition formats with a little more manual input.
All of the examples in this article are from core scanned by the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) here.
I have randomly chosen Hole NWG-05-03, box 303.
This is the hole. It is 13GB of SWIR data, be warned.

Opening raw data
CoreSpecViewer exposes a number of data open options through it’s load dialogue.







The CoreSpecViewer load dialogue.


Six different load modes

Open processed dataset
Open hole directory

These two refer to CoreSpecViewer’s own created data files, these files are what get saved after you have worked with a scan in the software.

Open raw dataset from Lumo output directory
Open raw dataset from individual ENVI files

These are for raw data from core scans. CoreSpecViewer will expect at least six files.








File
Extension
Description

metadata file - optional



As I built CoreSpecViewer to work with data from the Specim Lumo acquisition software, clicking “from Lumo output directory” just requires the whole output directory, and all of the file discovery is automated and the metadata is parsed nicely.
If your data was acquired any other way, or your directory structure got mangled, the “from ENVI files” allows you to browse to each required file. The XML will be brute force parsed, but maybe not effectively, and CoreSpecViewer will prompt for the required metadata (hole id, box number, from depth, to depth).

Open reflectance data

This button allows you to open a core scan that has already been converted to reflectance and stored in an ENVI file. It will also support existing masks (depending on the format).

Open archive file

This is another file type produced by CoreSpecViewer, the need for which is discussed in this note


Pre-processing raw data
With hyperspectral data, you cannot just open the file and start interpreting the data, that would be far too easy. The cameras themselves will usually handle some geometric corrections, any spectral binning and some other correction before you get any data.
That just leaves correcting the radiance data to reflectance, which is why 6 files are needed.
\[
Reflectance = \frac{Data-DarkReference}{WhiteReference-DarkReference}
\]
BUT! CoreSpecViewer handles all of this for you! If you want to see the implementation it is here
Simply find your directory, or selection of files, click load and voilà







A reflectance corrected core box, at the click of a button


As this is python application, all of the details of the reflectance correction performed are in the source and parts of the configuration is adjustable in the UI. All of the configuration is adjustable in the source code.
This raw data can be cropped in the UI, a mask can be created using a variety of methods, and the pre-processing pipeline completed with a few button clicks:







View of the visualise window after masking tools have been used.


This image is fully interactive, and individual pixel spectra can be examined using mouse clicks.







Examine reflectance specrta or continuum-removed spectra


So far, so easy, but we haven’t actually learned anything about our core yet.
CoreSpecViewer has a number of tools to actually extract information from the core. I am not familiar with the geology of Alberta, or this drillhole, I am just using free data selected at random so…these interpretations will be less valid than those of a geologist who knows the geology!


Early exploration
I will perform a quick unsupervised clustering to see what variation my core has:







K-means output using 5 clusters for 50 iterations


I used the default settings of 5 clusters for 50 iterations (these will obviously need tweaking with geological knowledge). The image shows that the core is dominated by 3 main mineralogical domains (Classes 3, 2, and 1) with small distinct “blobs” of class 4. But what are the classes? How different are they?
We can interrogate the cluster centres:







Viewing the cluster centres as spectra


The spectra for Class 1 (blue line), Class 2 (orange line) and Class 3 (green line) are very similar. There are differences in intensity at shorter wavelengths (which explains the variation in the false colour image), but they all have the same features with varying depths. Class 4 (red line) is different, while it shares the shorter wavelength features as the other classes, it has a distinctly different feature around 2335nm.
Now that we know a little bit more about the spectral variation in the core, we can try to simply match these cluster centres to spectra from the Ecostress library.
Note, I didnt save the data, and when I came back to it I had to start from raw, thus a different mask and the clustering came out differently. Don’t be me, the save button is right there!







Cluster centre table after matching against library spectra using three metrics


The direct library matches are giving us a mixture of usefully recognised minerals and nonsense. The matches have been performed using three different metrics; Pearson correlation, Spectral Angle Mapping and Modified Spectral Angle Mapping.
Class 4 is confidently identified as Calcite by two of the three metrics, and Classes 2 and 3 are identified as Montmorillonite. Class 1 is identified as elemental Sulfur by the Pearson correlation which is…unlikely. This class is clearly being matched on noise, and doesn’t reach the threshold for identification in the other two methods.
We can also just directly compare each individual spectra against the library directly, using any of the three techniques to produce a mineral map.







Direct mineral mapping against full library


Again a mixture of usefully recognised minerals and nonsense.


Take-Away
In under 10 minutes, without writing code, we can open, correct and interpret hyperspectral core scanning data, easily!
I can confidently say that there is probably some carbonate in discrete areas and the rest is probably some kind of clay or mica, and the key scientific conclusion in everything ever done: Further work is needed.
To go further, and be more confident in your interpretations you will need to;

examine the individual features (tools exist in CoreSpecViewer),
curate the library to ensure matches are checked against realistic options (tools exist in CoreSpecViewer),
use your own library (open it in CoreSpecViewer),
select spectra from your data and build your own library (tools exist in CoreSpecViewer).

That’s the point: Hyperspectral interpretation still requires geologists, not just algorithms — but the barrier to entry shouldn’t be the software.
If you have hyperspectral core scanning data in raw Lumo output files, check out CoreSpecViewer and send me all your complaints!
If you have hyperspectral core scanning data from other acquisition methods, let’s see if we can collaborate to extend CoreSpecViewer to smooth file discovery and metadata parsing!
If you don’t have any data, but want to play with the software, there are links to some open source data on the GitHub landing page.
